title: Performance and the instruction cycle
subtitle: How to say a computer is “fast” with a number, and what the processor actually does between two ticks.

orgarch.title: Organisation versus architecture
orgarch.body:
Computer architecture is what a programmer can see: the instruction set, registers, addressing modes and data types. Computer organisation is how it is built to provide that: control signals, buses, cache design, the technology. Two machines with the same architecture (two x86 chips) can have very different organisations — and different speeds.

A computer is a processor that fetches instructions and data from memory, with I/O to the outside world, joined by a bus. A multi-core processor simply puts several processors on one chip sharing the memory system.

cycle.title: The instruction cycle
cycle.body:
Every instruction goes through the same loop: fetch it from the address in the program counter, decode what it asks for, execute it (possibly fetching operands and writing a result), then advance the program counter. A jump simply loads a new address into the counter. Interrupts are checked between instructions.

Watch an Intel 8085 do exactly this: each step is one instruction, the highlighted row is the one about to run, and the registers and flags change beneath.

perf.title: Measuring performance
perf.body: Execution time = instruction count × CPI (cycles per instruction) × clock period. The clock rate is only one of the three factors; a faster clock with a worse CPI can be slower. MIPS = instruction count / (time × 10⁶) = clock rate / (CPI × 10⁶), but MIPS misleads across different instruction sets.
perf.steps: A 2 GHz processor runs a program of 10⁹ instructions at CPI 1.5. Cycles = instructions × CPI. Time = cycles / clock. MIPS = clock / (CPI × 10⁶).

amdahl.title: Amdahl's law
amdahl.body: Speeding up only a fraction f of a program by a factor s gives overall speed-up 1 / ((1 − f) + f/s). The serial part (1 − f) caps everything: even with infinite s the limit is 1/(1 − f). This is why adding cores helps a little for mostly-serial programs.
amdahl.steps: A program spends 80% of its time in a part that can be made 4× faster. Apply the law.

risc.title: RISC and CISC
risc.body: CISC machines (x86) have many complex, variable-length instructions, some of which do a lot of work. RISC machines (ARM, RISC-V, MIPS) have few, simple, fixed-length instructions, use load/store for all memory access and keep many registers — which makes pipelining easy. Berkeley RISC added overlapped register windows: each procedure gets a window of registers that overlaps its caller's, so parameters are passed without touching memory.

summary.title: Summary
summary.body:
• Architecture = visible contract; organisation = implementation.
  • Time = instructions × CPI × period.
  • Amdahl: the serial fraction limits speed-up.
  • The instruction cycle: fetch, decode, execute, repeat.
